title: Ash Wednesday: dust
hook: ashes on the forehead and the words: remember you are dust (Genesis 3:19)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Epiphany: strangers from the east, a river, a wedding. Your line was the light is for everyone. Now the circle turns darker.

One Wednesday in late winter or early spring, you might notice it on the train, at the office, in the grocery line: a dark smudge on someone's forehead. Sometimes a neat cross. Sometimes just a gray thumbprint. People who don't know lean over and say, hey, you've got something on your face. They know. It's there on purpose. That morning or at lunch, in a church, a minister or priest dipped a thumb in ash, pressed it to their forehead, and said a few words from the third chapter of Genesis, words about dust. A reminder worn in public, for one day. Today's word is the day it happens.
screen: `A SMUDGE ON THE TRAIN.` → `YOU'VE GOT SOMETHING ON YOUR FACE.` → `ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Ash Wednesday: the first day of Lent. Often the ashes come from burning the palm branches of last year's Palm Sunday, so last year's celebration becomes this year's dust. The words often echo what God says to Adam in Genesis. In the King James: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." That's blunt. Every life ends. In the Bible, ashes go with grief and turning around: Job, at the end of his long argument with God, says he repents "in dust and ashes." But go back one chapter in Genesis, to how the first human was made: "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life." Readers of the Hebrew hear a pun. The human is adam. The ground is adamah. An earthling, from the earth. So being dust isn't only bad news. It's what God picked up, and shaped, and breathed into. A psalm puts it tenderly: "he remembereth that we are dust." Not as a threat. As someone who knows how fragile you are. Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans and Methodists keep Ash Wednesday, and some other churches do too. Orthodox Christians don't; their Great Lent begins on a Monday called Clean Monday, after an evening when people ask one another's forgiveness. For Christians, the ash points two ways: you are dust, and you are loved.
screen: `LAST YEAR'S PALMS, BURNED.` · `DUST THOU ART.` · `ADAM FROM ADAMAH.` · then, large: `HE REMEMBERETH THAT WE ARE DUST.` · then: `DUST, AND BREATHED INTO.`

segments.voice: Press a finger into a plant's soil, touch the earth outside, or just look closely at the back of your hand, and remember you're made of the same stuff as the ground. You won't be here forever; let that be true without panicking, and feel your breath going in and out. If you pray, remember the other half, breathed into and loved; if you don't, simply hold both at once: fragile, and here.
Ash Wednesday. The first day of Lent, when Christians in a number of churches receive ashes on the forehead and hear that they are dust. Today's word.
Your line: dust, and loved. Last year's palms, this year's ash. One hundred thirteen days now.

notes: 'Forty-six days before Easter': Lent's forty days plus the six Sundays, in Western reckoning. Confirm.

The imposition formula varies (e.g. 'Remember that you are dust...' or 'Repent, and believe the Gospel'); script says the words 'echo' Genesis 3:19 in many churches. Modern liturgical wording is not quoted.
Ashes from the previous year's palms: common practice, not universal. Stated as 'usually'. Confirm.
Orthodox: Great Lent begins on Clean Monday, after Forgiveness Sunday Vespers. Confirm.
The adam/adamah wordplay is standard; 'earthling' is a common gloss. Confirm.
